rows.description: A child whose parents respond only to marks feels loved for performance and hides mistakes; the harm is less the standard than the sense that love depends on meeting it.
A classmate notices the topper who cannot enjoy results and gets anxious over a single mark. Being kind, not hating on their success, and inviting them to relax can lessen the isolation.
A teenager delays a project because a poor result would reveal weakness; putting it off protects the self-image but makes the eventual work worse.
Building diligent study routines, punctuality, and academic honesty vs. procrastination, slacking off, and cheating.

rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.

rows.subtype: Groaning, moaning and huffing at demands [Expressing]
rows.description: A teenager groans at homework or chores, meaning boredom, protest or stress. It rarely means real refusal; a light response and a clear expectation works better than a lecture, while a groan of real pain should be taken seriously.

rows.subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager describes a friend as perfect one week and as a total traitor the next after a small slight; strong feelings make it hard to hold both good and disappointing sides together.
A child says, "You have it now, I have it after lunch." Splitting the time between them ends the shouting with each getting a turn.

A young adult delays starting a project or applying for jobs because the result may not be flawless. Either everything is perfect or it is worthless, so little gets finished.
